rejected.title: Evaluating an inquiry
card: Evaluating means judging how well an inquiry worked. It is the last step, and it also says what could be done better next time.

rejected.remember: Check the data is reliable and enough, check for bias, then say how to improve.

a.q: Which question would a student ask to check whether data is reliable?
opts: Would collecting it again give similar results?
Was the data shown in a graph?
Did the inquiry start with a question?
Was the data collected in a nearby place?
a.why: Reliable data gives similar results when collected again in the same way. A graph, a starting question or a nearby place do not show that results would repeat.
a.clue: Think about repeating the data collection.

b.q: Priya picks 6 households at random from across Parramatta and asks how each person gets to work. Four say they drive, so she concludes most residents drive. What is the best evaluation?
opts: The sample was too small, so the data is not enough
The sample was biased, so the conclusion is unfair
The data is reliable, so the conclusion is secure
The data is enough, so no improvement is needed
b.why: Six households cannot show a pattern for a suburb of thousands of people, so the sample was too small and the data is not enough. Bias is tempting, but she picked households at random from across the suburb, so no group or place was favoured. A larger sample would improve the inquiry.
b.clue: She chose the households fairly. What else can weaken a conclusion?

Reliable
the data would give similar results if it were collected again in the same way.

b.q: Priya surveys 6 people at one bus stop in Parramatta and concludes that most of the suburb's residents drive to work. What is the best evaluation of her inquiry?
opts: The data is not enough, so the sample was too small
The data is biased, so the survey should be repeated
The data is reliable, so the conclusion is secure
The data is enough, so no improvement is needed
b.why: Six people at one bus stop is too little data to show a pattern for a whole suburb. The tempting answer is bias, but nothing suggests a source gave one side unfairly. The problem is the amount of data.
b.clue: Count how many people she asked compared with the suburb.

problems.detail: Surveying people at a bus stop gives an unrepresentative sample, which is a form of bias. So the 'biased' option is defensible, and the why's claim that nothing suggests bias is wrong. The scenario is also odd: bus-stop users are unlikely to show that most residents drive. Choose a neutral survey site, such as a shopping centre, so only the sample size is at issue.
The clue 'Count how many people she asked compared with the suburb' points straight at sample size and gives the answer away.
The intended option reverses cause and effect: 'The data is not enough, so the sample was too small'. It should read that the sample was too small, so the data is not enough.
